note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old lawyer with new-onset, work-associated frontal headaches plus palpitations, shortness of breath at rest, and bilateral hand tingling; reduced appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, and decreased libido since a job change. Impression: work-related stress/anxiety with hyperventilation vs thyroid dysfunction; plan for in-person exam and thyroid labs.

History:
- Presenting complaint/timeline:
  - Headaches: severe, frontal, occur mainly at work (meetings/laptop); not typically on commute; mild nausea at times; patient did not have frequent headaches prior to this.
  - Palpitations: ~once daily or more, sometimes triggered in the elevator in the morning.
  - Dyspnea: at rest while sitting at desk; not with exercise.
  - Tingling: bilateral hands; described as tingling/prickling.
  - Appetite/weight: reduced appetite with ~5 lb unintentional weight loss; no clear change in clothing fit; no external comments on weight.
  - Libido: decreased; onset aligned with job change.
  - Onset/progression: began around time of changing jobs; symptoms occur at different times (not all together); significant work-related stress (rated 7–8/10).
- Pertinent negatives (as stated):
  - Dyspnea not with exercise.
  - No regular prior headaches before current episode.
- Past medical history:
  - “Hyperthyroidism” reported by patient.
- Medications:
  - Thyroxine (levothyroxine); reports good adherence.
- Allergies:
  - Not stated.
- Social:
  - Lawyer in London; approximately 50/50 meetings and computer work; high reading load.
  - Alcohol: a couple of glasses of wine once weekly.
  - Tobacco: none.
  - Recreational drugs: denies.
- Preventive/other:
  - None mentioned.

Examination:
- No in-person exam performed (tele-visit).
- No vitals recorded.
- Plan stated to examine heart and breathing at in-person visit.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression:
  1) Work-related anxiety/panic with hyperventilation (high likelihood): Onset with new, stressful job; symptoms mostly at work; elevator trigger; dyspnea at rest (desk) but not with exertion; bilateral hand tingling and palpitations consistent with hyperventilation/anxiety; reduced appetite, mild weight loss, and decreased libido commonly associated with stress.
  2) Thyroid dysfunction (possible iatrogenic hyperthyroidism from levothyroxine over-replacement) (medium likelihood): On thyroxine with weight loss, palpitations, anxiety-like symptoms, and decreased libido. Needs biochemical confirmation.
  3) Tension-type headache related to stress/ergonomics (medium likelihood): Frontal headaches during work and screen use; high occupational stress; minimal migrainous features.
- Other considerations (lower likelihood): Workplace indoor air quality/CO exposure (headaches mainly at work), anemia or B12 deficiency (paresthesias, palpitations), though timing with job change favors stress-related causes.

Plan:
- In-person evaluation:
  - Full set of vitals (including BP and HR) and cardiorespiratory exam as discussed.
  - Neurologic screening exam (given headaches and paresthesias).
- Labs:
  - Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4 ± free T3) to assess current replacement status, as planned.
  - Consider CBC, ferritin, and vitamin B12 given paresthesias, palpitations, and weight/appetite changes (consistent with differential).
- No medications initiated prior to in-person assessment.
- Symptom management and monitoring:
  - Headache diary; optimize hydration, regular meals, and scheduled screen breaks; review workstation ergonomics.
  - Breathing techniques for episodes (if hyperventilation suspected) and discussion of potential triggers (elevator, meetings).
- Mental health screening/management:
  - Consider GAD-7/PHQ-9 at visit; discuss stress-reduction strategies and possible counseling if indicated.
- Cardiac rhythm assessment:
  - Consider ECG if palpitations persist or are worsening.
- Occupational/environmental:
  - At visit, consider asking about coworkers with similar symptoms and workplace ventilation/CO alarms if symptoms remain predominantly at work.
- Follow-up:
  - Patient to book an in-person clinic appointment via the app as advised.
  - Reassess after exam and labs; adjust thyroid medication only based on results.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements:
  - Exact duration and frequency details for each symptom; headache red flags (photophobia, phonophobia, aura, neck stiffness, focal deficits), vision changes.
  - Allergy status clarification.
  - Full medication list with dosages; exact thyroxine dose and timing.
  - Vitals and physical exam; formal anxiety/depression screening; caffeine and sleep history.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Patient reports “hyperthyroidism” but is taking thyroxine (replacement) — conflict noted; requires verification.
  - “Feeling hot” listed initially; patient later emphasized shortness of breath rather than heat intolerance — minor discrepancy.
● Transcript quality:
  - Some responses incomplete/garbled; several clarifying questions left unanswered; no objective data available due to tele-visit.
